description: The standard rule's file set: which files RetroArch writes for a core on a system, declared from the frontend's naming rule and the core's own source rather than read off the save directory. Three things these vectors pin. That the answer is a DECLARATION: a file lying under the content's stem which this core cannot write is not reported, because it is evidence about the past and the question is where this configuration writes now. That a record is keyed by core AND system: one mGBA answers a Game Boy cartridge's clock and a Game Boy Advance cartridge's not at all, so the same core states different sets for its two systems and states nothing at all where the system is unknown. And that the claim is pinned to the build it was read at, because a rebuild is exactly what can add or drop a memory id. A core with no record keeps the old answer — the directory resolves and the file set stays what it always was.

The result is the same string for ordinary content, which is why the answer states <rom_stem>.ngf — but the route matters for one case the card records: content whose whole path carries no dot gets no save file at all.

vectors.name: a-pocket-handheld-whose-core-writes-its-flash-into-the-standard-save-directory

vectors.name: the-colour-model-the-same-core-serves-answers-by-the-same-flash-rule

vectors.name: four-files-for-one-game-and-one-of-them-shares-the-frontends-name
vectors.rationale: Geolith writes four files of its own per game — the board's NVRAM, the cartridge RAM, a memory card and the CD backup RAM — into the frontend's own save directory. Three roles across four names, so a client can tell the memory card from the rest. The second name is why this is a card and not a record: for CD content the core also fills the save-RAM id, so RetroArch writes <rom_stem>.srm onto the same path the core writes at unload. Every other two-writer case read so far kept the two apart by name. The answer states the set either way, because the names are the core's and it writes them for cartridge content too.

vectors.name: the-last-emulator-a-system-offers-completes-it
vectors.rationale: Game Boy Advance is offered by five emulators and this is the fifth. Four of them fill the libretro save interface and RetroArch writes their file; NooDS fills none of it and keeps a <rom_stem>.sav of its own, opened as a descriptor the emulator writes into directly. Same directory, different writer, and with it every emulator the system offers answers — the fourth system to reach that, after Game Boy, Game Boy Color and Super Game Boy. The file is also created on first launch whether the game ever saves or not, which the card records and the answer does not need to: the set is what can be written, and this one always is.

vectors.name: retroarch-compressing-its-saves-leaves-no-file-a-fixed-size
vectors.rationale: save_file_compression is on in retroarch.cfg, so RetroArch writes the .srm and the .rtc it names as RZIP streams whose length follows their content. Gambatte reports a fixed size for both on a Game Boy cartridge, and the answer still says false for each, with one save-files-compressed caveat naming the key and the cfg it came from.

vectors.name: a-core-override-that-turns-compression-on-is-the-layer-named

vectors.name: a-cartridge-clock-and-its-save-each-keep-their-size
vectors.rationale: Gambatte fills both ids for a Game Boy cartridge, so the standard answer is two groups, one per file RetroArch writes: the .srm, sized by the RAM banks the header declares, and the .rtc, the clock's fixed structure. Both are fixed, and with compression at its default neither carries a caveat.

vectors.name: a-written-cartridge-save-keeps-its-size-claim-once-observed
vectors.rationale: The game has saved once, so the answer is an observation of the save directory rather than the card's declaration. The file it found is the one RetroArch writes through Genesis Plus GX's SRAM interface, and it answers exactly as it did before it existed: fixed, with the trailing-fill exception beside it, because the claim is about the file and not about whether it has been written yet.

data.citation: [V] libretro/libretro.c:3759-3784 at ekeeke/Genesis-Plus-GX 46a5521 — SAVE_RAM answers 0x10000 before emulation runs and, while it runs, the length up to the last byte that is not 0xff, so the file is the cartridge's 64 KiB SRAM less a trailing run of 0xff that moves with what the game has written.

vectors.name: compression-reaches-the-file-a-card-hands-the-frontend
vectors.rationale: A rule card's .srm that the core hands RetroArch through the SRAM interface is still a file RetroArch writes, so save_file_compression applies to it as it does to the standard rule's: the group is false, the caveat names the key, and the trailing-fill exception is not stated, because a compressed file has no fixed size to make an exception to.

vectors.name: a-per-game-cartridge-ram-keeps-the-size-its-name-carries
vectors.rationale: Genesis Plus GX writes both of a CD game's backup RAM files itself, so neither size comes from the frontend: the internal RAM is always 0x2000 bytes, and the cartridge RAM is as large as the cartridge size option, which is spelled into the file's name. So each name always holds one size, and both groups say size_fixed true from the card's sizes block (#681 D9, D11).

vectors.name: bsnes-jg-states-the-frontends-srm-and-its-own-rtc-as-two-groups

The two files have different writers, so the card states one group per file and each says its own size: the .srm from the frontend's claim, the .rtc from the card's sizes block (#681 D13).
